context_needed: The regressor is residence in the Africare region, where access to the Burundi ex-combatant reintegration programme was disrupted (pp. 16-17, Appendix B pp. 50-52); the comparison is non-Africare ex-combatants with uninterrupted access. So the printed coefficient and OR are the effect of NOT having the programme; the authors read OR 0.49-0.26 as 51-74% lower odds among Africare respondents (p. 27). 'Matching & regression' is the reduced form, presented as a lower bound; the 'het. exposure adjustment' scales it by the 0.53 disruption rate and is presented as an upper bound (pp. 17, 52). 'No adjustment' is the raw, unmatched comparison (N 371). Outcomes are binary indicators defined on pp. 27-28.

rule: When a table prints a logit coefficient and its odds ratio side by side, store one row per outcome and specification with effect_type 'odds ratio' and the OR as printed; the s.e. column belongs to the coefficient, not the OR. Read which group the indicator codes before reading the direction of the effect. When the regressor is the comparison condition (here disrupted access), store the ratio in the programme-vs-comparison direction: the reciprocal of the printed OR, with the printed value in note.

resolved_questions.question: (1) Direction: the regressor is disrupted access, so the printed OR is comparison-over-programme. The reversed-convention rule says flip the sign of a difference, but for a ratio the flip is the reciprocal (e.g. 0.49 -> 2.04), which the rules do not settle; rows keep the value as printed and say so in the note. (2) The authors call the matching-and-regression and the exposure-adjusted estimates the lower and upper bounds of the effect. These are not Lee/Manski bounds; rows store them as two specifications rather than as bound_lower/bound_upper on one row.
resolved_questions.resolution: Decided by Lucas, 22 Nov 2026: flip ratios to the programme-vs-comparison direction (reciprocal), keeping the printed value in note.
